newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban vows not to repeat costly mistake.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban vows not to repeat costly mistake.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia said on Saturday it was planning house-to-house searches for civilian arms in villages it has just conquered -- avoiding a costly mistake it made last year.

"Our operation against the Panjsher (valley) and (the main northern town of) Mazar-i-Sharif will continue to root out the enemy, but first we want to collect all arms from the areas which we captured recently," a Taleban commander said.
Panjsher is the stronghold of the ousted government's military commander Ahmad Shah Masood and Mazar-i-Sharif is the base of powerful Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The Taleban seized the strategic Bagram airbase and the Parwan province capital of Charikar, north of the capital Kabul, on Thursday and went on to take parts of the nearby Kapisa province, including its capital Mahmud-i-Raqi on Friday.

The mainly ethnic Pashtun militia had captured all these areas soon after taking Kabul in late September but was pushed out in a counter-offensive by Masood's forces, helped by the non-Pashtun local population.

On Saturday the Taleban forces were at Deh Bali, 75 km (45 miles) from Kabul and only 15 km (10 miles) from Panjsher, where Masood earned his fame for leading guerrilla attacks against Soviet occupation forces in the 1980s.

"The villagers of Parwan and Kapisa misused our goodwill when we captured these areas last year but did not bother to make house-to-house search for weapons," Taleban frontline commander Haji Feda Mohammad told reporters.
In their last drive in October, the Taleban forces, which now control about two-thirds of Afghanistan, apparently did not fully consider a possible insurgency by armed villagers.
"We know our enemy now and need to disarm them, and if we don't then they will ambush us," Feda Mohamnmad said.
Speaking in a restaurant in Deh Bali's deserted bazaar, he said the Taleban was serious about disarming locals and then marching forward for the next battle.
Outside the restaurant, as snow fell, delegates from several areas of Kapisa province waited to talk to Feda Mohammad on a peaceful deal on disarming villagers.

"We don't want to have any confrontation with the Taleban operation against Masood and Dostum," said an old man speaking for Kapisa's Kohistan area. "All we have come here for is to say that our sons and relatives are all ready to surrender their weapons if there is no Taleban punishment."
Another delegate said his people would give guarantees guarantee against any anti-Taleban ambushes from their villages.

"We will not allow any of those fugitives to enter our village for attacking the Taleban," said Ghulam Yahya, who shivered with cold and wore a white turban in an apparent move to appease the Taleban, whose fighters carry white flags.
Most civilians feared the Taleban might order them to evacuate their villages to guard against ambushes.

"Taleban have told us leave our houses and we don't have anywhere to go. We have no cash and all we have got are Dostum's banknotes which are not valid in Taleban's teritory," a villagers from Bagram area said.
But Amir Khan Mutaqi, the Taleban government's acting Information and Culture Minister, said the government had taken no such decision yet.
Many displaced people along the freezing plain on Saturday headed towards Kabul carrying belongings on animals or a few available trucks.
